note: Where the Surveyor hides in each snapshot. Each spot is tied to something happening there during that era. Keys are snapshot years. 'hint' is a vague region, offered on request.

-123000.note: Ochre engraved with cross-hatching here, about 75,000 years ago, is among the oldest known human art.

-10000.note: Settled by about 9000 BCE, Jericho is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places on Earth.

-8000.note: A town of thousands with no streets: people walked across the roofs and climbed down ladders into their homes.

-5000.note: Graves here, from around 4500 BCE, hold the oldest worked gold yet found.

-4000.note: Uruk grew into perhaps the first true city, and its scribes into some of the first writers.

-3000.note: A Neolithic village in Orkney with stone beds and dressers, older than Stonehenge and the pyramids.

-2000.note: An Indus Valley port with what may be the world's oldest known dock.

-1500.note: The Hittite capital, whose archives held thousands of clay tablets, including the earliest known peace treaty text.

-1000.note: The Olmec carved colossal stone heads here, some weighing over twenty tonnes.

-700.note: King Ashurbanipal's library here preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh on clay tablets.

-500.note: Confucius taught here; he died in 479 BCE, his ideas eventually shaping Chinese government for two thousand years.

-400.note: Socrates was tried and sentenced to death in Athens in 399 BCE.

-323.note: Alexander the Great died here in 323 BCE, aged 32; his empire split among his generals.

-300.note: Ships docking at Alexandria were searched for books, which were copied for the library.

-200.note: A decree issued in 196 BCE was carved in three scripts; found here in 1799, it unlocked hieroglyphs.

-100.note: Spartacus broke out of a gladiator school here in 73 BCE and led an army of escaped slaves.

-1.note: A busy Roman town of perhaps 11,000 people, a few decades before Vesuvius.

100.note: Begun in 122 CE across the width of Britain, marking the empire's northern edge.

200.note: A caravan city whose queen, Zenobia, would soon defy Rome.

300.note: Aksum minted its own coins, traded across the Red Sea, and raised stone stelae over 20 metres tall.

400.note: Founded in the 5th century, Nalanda became one of the world's first great residential universities.

500.hint: a valley in the Hindu Kush
500.note: Giant Buddhas were carved into the cliffs here in the 6th century; they were destroyed in 2001.

600.note: The Tang capital, laid out on a grid, was probably the largest city in the world.

700.note: Scholars in Abbasid Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Indian works and built on them.

800.note: Charlemagne's court gathered scholars who standardised a clear script: the ancestor of our lowercase letters.

900.note: Capital of al-Andalus, with paved, lit streets and a library said to hold 400,000 volumes.

1000.note: Norse sailors built turf halls here around 1000 CE, five centuries before Columbus.

1100.note: Cahokia's builders also raised a ring of posts, nicknamed Woodhenge, to track the solstices.

1200.note: The Southern Song capital had more than a million people, paper money and restaurants with menus.

1279.note: Marco Polo would return here in 1295 with stories few believed.

1300.note: Dante was writing the Divine Comedy, in Italian rather than Latin, around 1308–1321.

1400.note: Ulugh Beg's observatory here measured the length of the year to within a minute, in the 1420s.

1492.note: Granada surrendered to Castile in January 1492; months later Columbus sailed under the same monarchs.

1500.note: Visitors compared the capital of this South Indian empire to Rome.

1530.note: The Inca capital, months before Pizarro's men arrived in 1533.

1600.note: The battle here in 1600 led to the Tokugawa shogunate and over 250 years of peace.

1650.note: Home of the world's first stock exchange and the busiest port in Europe.

1700.note: The Safavid capital was so splendid a proverb said 'Isfahan is half the world'.

1715.note: Founded in 1703 on a marsh by Peter the Great, and capital of Russia from 1712.

1783.note: The US Constitution was drafted here in 1787, in a room with the windows shut for secrecy.

1800.hint: the mouth of the Columbia River
1800.note: Lewis and Clark wintered here in 1805–06 after crossing the continent.

1815.note: Napoleon's final defeat, on 18 June 1815; Wellington called it 'the nearest-run thing'.

1878.note: Edison's lab demonstrated a long-lasting electric light bulb here in 1879.

1880.note: Meiji Japan was building railways, a constitution and a modern army at remarkable speed.

1900.note: Fifty million visitors saw talking films, escalators and the Grand Palais.

1914.note: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was shot near this bridge on 28 June 1914, after his driver took a wrong turn.

1920.note: Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, almost untouched for 3,000 years.

1930.note: Carved between 1927 and 1941, largely with dynamite.

1938.note: Codebreakers here read German Enigma traffic, an effort kept secret until the 1970s.

1945.note: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached the summit on 29 May 1953.

1960.note: Apollo 11 launched from here in July 1969; its guidance computer had about 4 KB of memory.

1994.note: Opened in 1994, joining Britain to the continent by rail for the first time since the Ice Age land bridge.

2000.note: The 2008 Olympics opened at 8 pm on 8 August 2008, eight being a lucky number.

2010.note: The Large Hadron Collider confirmed the Higgs boson in 2012, 27 km of tunnel under two countries.
